title: "The hypergeometric distribution"
execute:
  enabled: true

The [binomial distribution](binomial-distribution.qmd) describes a fixed number
of independent trials with the same success probability. A fixed sample drawn
[**without replacement**](https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/4-5-hypergeometric-distribution)
from a finite linguistic table behaves differently: after one row has been
selected, that row cannot be selected again, and the balance of the remaining
rows changes. The [**hypergeometric distribution**](https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/4-5-hypergeometric-distribution)
represents this sampling procedure.

We define the finite Turkish morphology population and its fixed sample, derive the without-replacement mass and moments, and then contrast their variance with an independent-draw binomial reference.

Here **population** means the complete 588-row resource-defined set, and
[**sample**](https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-1-definitions-of-statistics-probability-and-key-terms)
means the 120 rows selected from it by the stated design. The later <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
[populations-and-samples page](../statistical-inference/populations-and-samples.qmd)
develops the distinction between a finite data resource and a broader target
process.

## A finite Turkish morphology population

We use [this version of the Turkish UniMorph data](https://github.com/unimorph/tur/tree/6c179ace7d2f3d7f3484020e5304c1544d07bb6b). Pimentel et al. ([2021](https://aclanthology.org/2021.sigmorphon-1.25/)) describe the morphological-reinflection task and Turkish expansion; Batsuren et al. ([2022](https://aclanthology.org/2022.lrec-1.89/)) describe the type-level UniMorph representation. The data are CC BY-SA 3.0.

The analyzed population retains the distinct Turkish verb lemmas with one form in the feature cell `V;IND;PST;3;SG;POS;DECL`. The [README for this version](https://github.com/unimorph/tur/blob/6c179ace7d2f3d7f3484020e5304c1544d07bb6b/README.md) says that verbs were generated semi-automatically and partially checked by a native speaker; unverified noun and adjective material is excluded. The preparation script derives `past_suffix` by taking the final two orthographic characters. UniMorph supplies the whole inflected form, so this operation does not recover an annotated morpheme boundary.

One population row maps the lemma *göndermek* ‘to send’ to *gönderdi* under the
feature bundle `V;IND;PST;3;SG;POS;DECL`, which denotes a positive declarative
third-person singular past indicative verb. The derived ending is *di*, so
`t_initial = 0`. In the fixed sample, *hata yapmak* maps to *hata yaptı* and has
the derived ending *tı*, so `t_initial = 1`. These are lemma–form records, not
corpus occurrences.

The sample file is a simple random sample of 120 distinct rows drawn without
replacement from all 588 population rows, using seed 414. We fix 120 before
drawing so that the sample contains about one fifth of the population: large
enough to compare empirical counts while leaving enough unselected rows for
without-replacement depletion to matter. No optimization over sample sizes
selects this value. Because the population is finite and each row can appear at
most once, drawing one lemma changes the composition available for the next
draw.

```{r}
#| label: load-unimorph-hypergeometric
library(ggplot2)

population <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-population.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
sample_120 <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-sample-120.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

N <- nrow(population)
K <- sum(population$t_initial)
n <- nrow(sample_120)
x_observed <- sum(sample_120$t_initial)
p_population <- K / N
finite_population_correction <- (N - n) / (N - 1)

support <- max(0L, n - (N - K)):min(n, K)
reference <- data.frame(t_initial_count = support)
reference$without_replacement <- dhyper(support, m = K, n = N - K, k = n)
reference$independent_draw <- dbinom(support, size = n, prob = p_population)

hyper_mean <- n * p_population
hyper_variance <- n * p_population * (1 - p_population) * finite_population_correction
binomial_variance <- n * p_population * (1 - p_population)

stopifnot(
  N == 588L, K == 200L, n == 120L, x_observed == 42L,
  !anyDuplicated(population$lemma),
  all(sample_120$lemma %in% population$lemma),
  abs(sum(reference$without_replacement) - 1) < 1e-12
)

data.frame(N, K, n, x_observed, hyper_mean, hyper_variance,
           binomial_variance, finite_population_correction)
```

## Mass, mean, and variance

If a population contains $N$ entries, $K$ carry a focal property, and $n$ entries are sampled without replacement, then the focal count $X$ has mass

$$
\mathbb{P}(X=x)
=\frac{\binom Kx\binom{N-K}{n-x}}{\binom Nn}.
$$

The support respects both finite stocks:

$$
\max\{0,n-(N-K)\}
\leq x\leq
\min\{n,K\}.
$$

The numerator counts samples containing $x$ focal entries and $n-x$ other entries; the denominator counts all size-$n$ samples.

More explicitly, choose $x$ of the $K$ focal rows and $n-x$ of the $N-K$
nonfocal rows. Multiplying those counts enumerates samples with exactly $x$
focal rows. Dividing by the $\binom Nn$ equally likely size-$n$ subsets turns
that count into a probability.

Its [expectation](expected-values.qmd) is the same as that of a binomial count with $p=K/N$, but its [variance](variance-and-covariance.qmd) contains the **finite-population correction**:

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=n\frac KN,
$$

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=n\frac KN\left(1-\frac KN\right)\frac{N-n}{N-1}.
$$

The correction is below one because the draw indicators are negatively
associated: selecting a focal row removes it and makes later focal selections
slightly less likely. The binomial variance omits this depletion because its
draws have constant success probability.

For the fixed sample, the expected number of *t*-initial endings is `r sprintf("%.3f", hyper_mean)`. The without-replacement variance is `r sprintf("%.3f", hyper_variance)`, smaller than the independent-draw variance of `r sprintf("%.3f", binomial_variance)`.

```{r}
#| label: plot-unimorph-hypergeometric
#| fig-cap: "Without-replacement and independent-draw reference masses for the Turkish UniMorph sample. The vertical line marks the fixed sample count."
reference_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(count = support, probability = reference$without_replacement,
             design = "without replacement"),
  data.frame(count = support, probability = reference$independent_draw,
             design = "independent draws")
)

ggplot(reference_long, aes(count, probability, color = design, linetype = design)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = x_observed, color = "grey25", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("without replacement" = "#8B1A1A",
                                "independent draws" = "grey45")) +
  labs(x = "t-initial forms in the fixed sample", y = "Probability",
       color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The finite population contains the 588 lexeme–paradigm rows in this UniMorph
cell. Repeated samples therefore vary over those 588 rows. Token frequencies <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
from Turkish speech or writing never enter the sampling procedure, so the
result describes samples from the table rather than patterns of Turkish usage.

## Check your understanding

1. Compute the probability of the observed count with `dhyper()`.
2. Explain why the two models have the same expectation but different variances.
3. What happens to the correction as $n/N$ approaches one?
4. Why would a corpus-token claim be unsupported by this population?
5. A student fits a binomial model directly to `sample_120`. Which assumption
   of that model conflicts with the sampling protocol?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The probability of the observed count is `dhyper(42, 200, 388, 120) = 0.082787`. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Both models have $\mathbb{E}[X]=nK/N=40.816327$, but sampling without replacement multiplies the binomial variance by the finite-population correction 0.797274. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. As $n/N$ approaches one, $(N-n)/(N-1)$ approaches zero and the sampling variance collapses because nearly the whole finite population is observed. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The population consists of 588 distinct UniMorph verb lemmas in one feature cell, not tokens sampled from Turkish usage, so it cannot support a corpus-token claim. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. The rows were sampled without replacement, so the indicators do not have a
   constant independent success probability across draws.

</details>

The population in this analysis is the census of 588 resource-defined
lemma–form rows, from which 120 rows were sampled without <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
replacement. The hypergeometric variance records the resulting finite-
population dependence. The next two pages return to CMUdict and model ordered
waiting counts.
